entries.title: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend (Sept. 17)
entries.summary: Doomsday readings, Dancing on the Waterfront and more events for “These Distracted Times.”
entries.content:
Thursday 


Salsa Dancing on the Waterfront at The Wharf

608 Wharf St. SW, 6 p.m., free

Like a good cruise ship director, The Wharf keeps coming up with reasons for folks to mix and mingle on the water. Through Oct. 8, there will be free salsa lessons every Thursday at 6 p.m. led by instructors from Classé Dance Company, followed by open dancing with a DJ

Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor at Politics and Prose
5015 Connecticut Ave. NW, 7 p.m., free

You’ve heard of late-stage capitalism? Bad news: Canadian social commentators Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor think the U.S. has hit “End Times Facism.” The pair of “influential leftist thinkers,” as The New York Times calls them, will be at Politics and Prose to discuss their new book that provides, “a sobering, scary vision of contemporary political battles.” Note that Thursday is a big night for District book lovers: Politics and Prose is also hosting bestselling novelist Kristin Hannah (“The Women”) at Sixth & I, plus Jonathan Capehart will chat with Elizabeth Alexander at the MLK Library. 

More to explore: Guitarist Pat Metheny at Strathmore

Friday 


Gods, Goddesses and Lotus Eaters: A Hirshhorn Odyssey 

Hirshhorn Museum, Independence Ave and 7th Street, noon, free

Washington’s leading contemporary art museum hops on the Homer bandwagon with this free tour highlighting works in its collection that reference Greek mythology. Meet at the Hirshhorn welcome desk; no tickets required. On Saturday the museum gets kid-friendly by celebrating International Dot Day, with pointillistic art activities and special guest Peter H. Reynolds, author and illustrator of the bestselling picture book “The Dot.”

“Some Like It Hot” at Olney Theatre Center

2001 Olney-Sandy Spring Road, Olney, 7:30 p.m., Tickets from $76

Theater critics were initially skeptical when they heard the Marilyn Monroe/Jack Lemmon classic film was being adapted for the stage a few years ago, coming closely on the heels of “Mrs. Doubtfire” and “Tootsie,” two other movies featuring straight men in drag. But “Some Like It Hot,” turned out better than both of its predecessors, winning four Tony Awards in 2023. This weekend Olney Theatre Center becomes the first regional theater to produce this musical about 1930s tap-dancing cads who dress up as women to flee the mob. Previews begin Friday and the show continues through Nov. 8.

More to explore: Counterpoint Concerts opens its chamber music series at Dupont Underground

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Saturday


50th Annual Falls Church Festival

223 Little Falls St., Falls Church, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., prices vary

The best thing about the Falls Church Festival — besides the fact that it's now been around for 50 years — is that it’s fun regardless of how much time you have, how old you are or how much money you want to spend. Got an hour? Stop by the weekly farmers market and browse the tables set up by 85 local community groups and vendors. Got more time and money? Engage in Taste of Falls Church, or day drink in the beer garden. Have kids? Get in line for a $10 pony ride, check out some crafts or go on a scavenger hunt.

H Street Festival

H Street NE, 12 to 7 p.m., free

Good go-go is guaranteed at the annual street fair sometimes branded as “D.C.’s largest block party.” More than 500 restaurants, artists, nonprofits and District businesses set up tables along almost a mile of H Street NE, with entertainment stages dotting the way. Pro tips: Take a bus or Uber to Gallaudet University and walk. If you do drive, be aware of street closures and do not block driveways, alleys, etc. in the neighborhood.

More to explore: Free education program open house at Signature Theatre

Sunday 


Capital One Center Celebration of the Arts

Capital One Center Metro Park, Tysons, 12 to 5 p.m., free

The suburban arts venue hosts a two-day outdoor open house featuring live painting by local artists, music, food and exhibits curated by the Tephra Institute of Contemporary Arts, a Northern Virginia nonprofit that promotes the “combustibility of creativity.”

Capitol Hill Chamber Music Festival 

St. Mark’s Episcopal Church, 301 A St. SE, 7 p.m., suggested donation $20 

A unique tri-city model powers this festival dedicated to chamber music played on period instruments. The musicians will reprise each concert in Annapolis and Baltimore. The series kicks off with a concert called, “These Distracted Times.” Believe it or not, that title is not a reference to late-stage capitalism or end times facism, but a 1649 piece by Welsh composer Thomas Tomkins, who wrote his “A Sad Pavan for These Distracted Times” after the execution of King Charles I. The festival continues at area churches through Oct. 9.

More to explore: Soul songstress Erykah Badu at Wolf Trap.

entries.title: Even With McConnell Back, Farm Bill Faces Long Road Ahead
entries.summary: Political hurdles remain even if the Senate Agriculture panel sends the measure to the floor Wednesday.
entries.content:
Sen. Mitch McConnell's return to the Capitol this week gives Senate Republicans back the vote they were missing when their farm bill stalled in committee last month. It doesn't give them a deal.

The Kentucky Republican, back after a three-month absence following a June fall, cast his first Senate vote Monday. “I’m here to work on the farm bill,” McConnell said Tuesday.

Senate Agriculture Chairman John Boozman has scheduled the committee to reconvene Wednesday afternoon to try again to advance the Agricultural Act of 2026, the same package that failed on a party-line 10-11 vote in August because of McConnell’s absence.

But the fate of the farm bill remains uncertain, along with the future of its programs and funding that are essential to the agricultural industry, as farmers are squeezed financially by tariffs, higher input prices — including major cost increases for diesel and fertilizer prices — and extreme weather and drought.

It’s unclear how Republicans could get Democratic support to pass the Senate version on the floor, or whether the Senate and House can work out differences between the two chambers’ versions of the measure.

Farmers from across the country have descended on D.C. this week to encourage lawmakers to pass a bill. Congress has extended the 2018 version of the farm bill as a stopgap, which means commodity prices have not been updated to match inflation, so farmers receive only about 80% of every dollar they are intended to receive in subsidies.

That extension runs out September 30, but most programs will be funded through the end of the year.

Aaron Heley Lehman, president of the Iowa Farmers Union, said farmers would be extremely discouraged if Congress is unable to help them when they need it most.

“They need help with rising input prices, with chaotic markets and with less support from USDA offices. All those things going against them and we can’t have our policy leaders come together and create a comprehensive farm bill to provide some stability,” Lehman said. “We’re getting a sense that they are hearing from constituents, but we haven’t seen that translate into action.”

Boozman has stressed that farmers' input and experiences directly shaped the legislation.

The Senate’s farm bill “is about giving the people who produce our food, protect our land and sustain our rural communities the tools and certainty they need to succeed,” Boozman said in a statement. “The committee must advance this bill, and I look forward to doing so this week.”

Even with full attendance, the committee's Republicans and Democrats remain stuck on the same fight that sank the bill in August: how long to delay a new requirement that states pick up part of the cost of SNAP benefits. Boozman has offered a one-year delay; ranking member Amy Klobuchar and Senate Democrats have held firm on two years.

Klobuchar and Democrats argue it's unfair to reward states with high payment-error rates with more time than everyone else, pointing to a deal made during the passage of the One Big Beautiful bill last year. Alaska, which has the highest error rates in the country, received a carve-out to garner the vote of Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska).

Klobuchar’s office did not respond to a request for comment, but there’s no indication that the Democrats’ stance on the SNAP cost shifts has changed.

The bill needs 60 votes to clear a filibuster — a bar Republicans can't hit on their own. Even if the Senate passes it, that version must be reconciled with the House-passed farm bill, which cleared the House in late April.

The biggest gap between the House and the Senate versions of the bill start with the SNAP cost shift, with the House version not including any cost shift delay. The House also removed a provision allowing year-round sales of E15 gasoline, something members from both parties want to be included in farm bill, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune.

The bill has also faced backlash from members of the Make America Healthy Again movement. A provision that would provide pesticide manufacturers important to the agriculture industry protection from lawsuits was stripped on the House floor. Another provision that pushes back the timeline for the EPA’s review of certain chemicals has also drawn ire from the MAHA crowd.

“The Farm Bill as it stands is anti-MAHA, whoever votes for it, should understand this,” Vani Hari, a MAHA influencer, said on X. “Call your Senator today - and have them vote no... Chemical companies will get another 5 year free pass with no review by the EPA!”

Agriculture staffers on both sides of the aisle are unsure where the bill will go next, with staffers telling The Washington Sun that it can't pass without an agreement on the SNAP debate.

“I think we’re all a bit confused about what’s next,” one agriculture staffer told The Sun.

entries.title: Barack Obama Announces the Death of His Family Dog Sunny
entries.summary: The Portuguese water dog joined the first family in 2013.
entries.content:
Sunny, the high-energy Portuguese water dog who rollicked through the White House during President Barack Obama’s second term in office, died this week, the Obama family announced on social media.

Sunny was 13 and remained “always loyal, always sweet, always ready for adventure, still fiery and gorgeous till the very end of her days,” Barack and Michelle Obama wrote Wednesday on social media.

Sunny entered the scene in August 2013 as the Obama family’s second presidential pet. She and her furry sibling Bo, who died of cancer in 2021, were both Portuguese water dogs, a hypoallergenic breed to accommodate Malia Obama’s allergies.

Sunny garnered a reputation as a mischievous pooch who, along with Bo, remained in high demand for visitor meet-and-greets. Michelle Obama acknowledged in 2015 that Sunny could, at times, be naughty and sneak off to defecate within the corridors of power. Sunny also reportedly bit an Obama family friend in face in 2017, a wound that required stitches by White House medical staff.

“Athletic and full of boundless energy, she leapt over the hedges on the South Lawn like they weren’t even there, chasing squirrels, birds and anything else that moved,” Barack and Michelle Obama said Wednesday. “And whereas the way to Bo’s heart usually involved a treat, Sunny was more interested in having us run around with her, roll on the floor with her, or have her belly rubbed for as long as we were willing.”
https://x.com/BarackObama/status/2100193157522620711?s=20The Obamas said Sunny loved their daughters, who famously begged the former president for a dog during his first presidential campaign in 2008.

“She had her eccentricities: other than Bo, she preferred people to dogs; she was a loud and sloppy drinker; and despite being a Portuguese Water Dog, she hated getting wet,” the announcement read. “We will miss her terribly, and imagine she’s with her big brother now, making sure he’s okay.”

entries.title: Republican Senators Say Even Their Trump-Loving Constituents Are Tired of the Iran War
entries.summary: Back after a five-week recess, the lawmakers say people at home are worried about rising prices as the fighting continues.
entries.content:
Republican senators returned to Washington this week, saying their constituents want answers about how President Donald Trump’s Iran war will end after more than six months of fighting.

“They don’t like it,” Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana) said of the people he spoke with back home. “Even the people that love the president don’t like it.”

While constituent complaints about rising prices were nearly universal during the lawmakers’ five-week recess, some Republicans said people in their state expressed concerns over the war’s duration, and others said voters want clarity about America’s goals in the conflict.

What Trump aims to get from Iran remains a mystery to many Texans, Sen. John Cornyn said of his conversations with constituents.

“If the president was clear on what the objectives were that we were trying to achieve, I think they would be more patient,” Cornyn said. “But in the absence of that, I think there’s just confusion.”

Sen. Thom Tillis said the war has become a top-three campaign issue in North Carolina, where the large military and veteran population has kept the war’s human cost at the forefront. Voters remain most focused on the economy, he said, but the war’s duration has made the lack of measurable progress harder to ignore.

For a war the Trump administration said would take weeks to complete, Sen. Mike Rounds said the months of back-and-forth attacks are wearing thin with folks in South Dakota.

“Most of them thought it would be quick in and out, similar to Venezuela, and that wasn’t the case,” he said.

Trump said last week that he expected the war to end “immediately after” the November elections. But senior advisers, including Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, have privately warned that Iran could resist through the remainder of Trump’s presidency.

Recent polling shows broad dissatisfaction with the war. An August UMass survey found that 54% of Americans disapproved of U.S. military actions in Iran, and nearly two-thirds disapproved of Trump’s handling of the war. And as inflation remains stubbornly high, driven by high energy costs stemming from fighting in the Middle East, 80% said the attack on Iran had increased gasoline and grocery prices.

“People are very, very concerned with the high price of gasoline, high price of diesel, high price of fertilizer, and I think they attribute that to the war,” said Sen. Rand Paul (R-Kentucky).

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who is locked in a fierce reelection battle against Democrat Troy Jackson, said she’s heard “a lot of concern” about the Strait of Hormuz and its impact on gas and diesel prices. Sen. Josh Hawley echoed those concerns, saying Missourians tended not to discuss Iran directly but repeatedly complained about rising costs.

“The conflict needs to come to a resolution,” Hawley said.

Those concerns now follow senators into another potential vote on the war.

The administration told Congress in a July 10 letter that hostilities had resumed July 7, and it considered the renewed fighting as the start of another 60-day period under the War Powers Resolution. That period has expired, and Congress still has not authorized the war.

The House passed its third Iran war powers resolution Tuesday, with seven Republicans joining Democrats, up from four in each of the previous two votes.

Tillis, who opposed the Senate’s last war powers push, said Tuesday that he plans to support the next resolution.

“It’s time to be clear on the strategic objectives and start measuring results,” Tillis said. “And that’s not something that we’ve had since they started the conflict.”

“You just can’t have some throwaway statement saying it’s going to end just after the election,” he added. “The American people are smarter than that.”

entries.title: Former D.C. Attorney General Crashes Protest to Defend Landlord
entries.summary: Karl Racine represents a developer being sued by D.C.’s current attorney general over poor housing conditions.
entries.content:
Lawyers are supposed to aggressively advocate for their clients in the courtroom. But on the sidewalk outside City Hall?

That’s what happened on Tuesday afternoon, when a fight over a lawsuit brought by D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb against a prominent D.C. developer accused of neglecting to maintain a residential building played out in full public view, led by an unexpected protagonist: Karl Racine, Schwalb’s predecessor and opponent in the litigation.

Racine verbally sparred with tenants who said they had experienced horrid housing conditions, and took pictures of tenants and organizers as they spoke during a protest against the developer — drawing accusations that he was being rude and a bully.

One council member called the sidewalk showdown “stunning,” while a council source who spoke on the condition of anonymity was less diplomatic: “Unhinged.” Robert White, the at-large council member who chairs the housing committee, admitted it was a novel experience. “I’ve never seen anything like that,” he said.

Racine — who, during his own term as D.C. attorney general, filed high-profile lawsuits against landlords — said he was simply going to bat for a client he said was being unfairly maligned for systemic housing issues across the city.

“I will defend a client to the hilt, in a legal and ethical way, and nothing I did today was illegal nor unethical,” he said.

The sidewalk conflict stemmed from Schwalb’s lawsuit filed earlier this month against Buwa Binitie, a well-connected and seasoned developer who has leveraged millions of dollars in public subsidies to build affordable housing across D.C.

In the legal claim, Schwalb says Binitie and his management company neglected the Delta Pearl, a 166-unit building at the east end of H Street NE, resulting in some 200 unabated housing code violations and conditions he called “shocking.” Schwalb is asking a D.C. judge to order that immediate repairs be made to the building.

In court filings, Racine and Binitie have said that some tenants have caused damage to the building, and attempts to make repairs have been stymied by threats from squatters. They have also argued that a large number of tenants have not been paying their rent, leaving the building with a $1.8 million operating deficit. On Tuesday, Racine, now a partner at Hogan Lovells Cadwalader, said there was evidence of an “organized, sustained effort to sabotage” the building.

“I know a slumlord case when I see one, and this isn’t that,” he said. “This is far more complicated.”

The tenants Racine engaged with, though, very much disagreed. They were holding a small news conference after wrapping up a lobbying day at the Wilson Building, where they met with lawmakers, pressing them to take action to combat bad housing conditions and to hold bad landlords accountable.

Nathan Hunter-El, an organizer with the tenant advocacy group Empower D.C., said he had formerly lived at Capitol Vista, another of Binitie’s buildings where there have been complaints of bad housing conditions.

“All these buildings are fucked up — you can excuse my French — and the tenants are suffering,” he said, while also explaining why some tenants have stopped paying rent. “Would you want to pay rent living in unhealthy and unsafe conditions?”

In 2021, in his final year as attorney general, Racine similarly recognized that D.C. law puts the onus on landlords to maintain their properties. “Our laws make clear that landlords and property managers have a legal responsibility to provide habitable living conditions to tenants,” he said at the time.

Racine said Tuesday that the situation with unpaid rent — and how it can affect a building’s financial sustainability — should require lawmakers to act. “I would argue the city council should be talking about what is necessary to ensure that these buildings get repaired,” he said.

White, who has passed bills to allow for speedier evictions, said that he understands that rent nonpayment remains a challenge for some landlords, which was especially true coming out of the pandemic. But he said that in some cases, that claim falls short.

“You are advertising luxury buildings, providing slum conditions, and claiming you can’t maintain the buildings because you have no money,” he told The Washington Sun. “And then we talk to [the Department of Housing and Urban Development] and find out they’ve given you millions of dollars, we look at District records and you get millions of dollars from there. The best-case scenario is you don’t know how to maintain your building, the worst-case scenario is you don’t want to do it.”

On top of the legal claims from Schwalb, Binitie is also facing a lawsuit brought by the co-owners of the Delta Pearl, who accuse him of “systematic mismanagement” of the building, including failures to make repairs and collect rent. A Virginia-based contractor is also suing his management company for not paying a $38,000 bill for repair work it did on the building.

Tenants and organizers are hoping to build political pressure against Binitie. They had asked lawmakers to reject a proposed land deal that would transfer a public parcel at the St. Elizabeths Hospital campus in Southeast to the developer. And they seemed to have succeeded: A planned hearing set for Wednesday to discuss the deal has been postponed.

Racine said he was just asking the council to hold off on casting judgement, political or otherwise, against Binitie until the legal process can play out.

“I ask everyone, including the members of the great D.C. Council, to hold their opinion in abeyance because guess what, there is a court process under way,” he said.

But even as the afternoon’s sparring came to an end, tenant organizers said they were rattled by his presence there.

“Both the level of direct intimidation and direct confrontation, and the fact that Karl Racine is a very public figure who has a reputation of litigating against slumlords,” said Farah Fosse of Empower D.C.

That fact also struck Starr Lindsay, a tenant of the Delta Pearl.

“You used to fight for people,” she told Racine.

“I still fight for people like you,” Racine replied. “I also represent clients who are honestly being accused of something that they are not guilty of. Don’t you think everybody deserves a day in court? We should just let the judge make the decision.”

The next court hearing is scheduled for Thursday.

entries.title: EU Wants Canada to Become the Bloc’s First Associate Member
entries.summary: Trump’s tariffs and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state have soured the relationship between the North American neighbors.
entries.content:
By Rob Gillies

STRASBOURG, France (AP) — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed making Canada the European Union’s first associate member, a striking overture as U.S. President Donald Trump’s threats drive Ottawa closer to Europe.

Trump’s tariffs and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state have soured the relationship between the North American neighbors. Canada is seeking to reduce its dependence on the United States, the destination for roughly 70% of its exports, and Prime Minister Mark Carney has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU.

In her annual State of the European Union address, von der Leyen said Canada and the EU would build on their existing free trade agreement, known as CETA, with a broader “Alliance for the Future” aimed at creating “a common prosperity and economic security space.”

She cast that closer relationship as rooted not just in trade but in shared democratic values.

“Above all, dear Mark, Europe and Canada believe in democracy,” von der Leyen said to Carney, who received a standing ovation at the European Parliament in Strasbourg. He is due to address the Parliament on Thursday.

A Canadian official familiar with the discussions told The Associated Press last week that Ottawa was exploring ties with the EU that could stop just short of membership. The official said Canada would seek an arrangement allowing its citizens to live and work in Europe without visas as part of a broader strategic partnership.

Carney’s office welcomed von der Leyen’s proposal, saying Canada was deepening ties with the EU “to strengthen our sovereignty” and supported a move beyond CETA.

Canada has already joined the EU's defense procurement program

Von der Leyen said the expanded partnership would cover advanced manufacturing, technology, defense production, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, cybersecurity and economic security.

“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said. “In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.”

Because Canada joining the EU as an associate member would be a first, there is no rulebook on how that would work or what it would mean in practice. It is unclear who would need to approve membership, and how long that could take.

Currently, all steps toward EU membership must be approved unanimously by the 27 member countries.

The idea of associate membership has been floated in the past for Ukraine, or for post-Brexit Britain, but no concrete steps have been taken.

The relationship between Canada and the European Union has reached a point where the two sides need to move beyond rhetoric and start building something more substantive, said Tobias Cremer, a German member of the European Parliament.

“Now is the time to stop sending each other love letters and put meat on the bone,” said Cremer, from the center-left Social Democrats.

He argued that any new arrangement should be more ambitious than another trade or defense agreement, describing the goal as a more holistic strategic alliance between Canada and the EU.

Existing frameworks such as CETA could provide a foundation, Cremer said, but should be used more fully and expanded. The case for closer ties, he said, is increasingly being driven by geopolitics as much as economics.

The aim, he said, should ultimately be bigger than a bilateral arrangement — potentially positioning the EU as a convener of middle powers, an idea Carney has also raised.

Canada this year became the first non-European country to join the EU’s 150-billion-euro ($173-billion) SAFE defense program, giving Canadian companies access to joint procurement as Europe seeks to increase its defense readiness.

Iratxe García Pérez, president of the Socialists & Democrats group in the European Parliament, praised Carney for showing “great courage confronting Donald Trump” and said allies were needed to defend “sovereignty, solidarity and international law.”

Carney said Tuesday that economic integration, once viewed largely as an asset, is increasingly “being used as a weapon by certain countries.” Discussions will ramp up at the Canada-EU summit in Montreal in late October, he said.

Carney has urged middle powers to work together

Canada has retaliated against U.S. tariffs and rejected trade terms Carney says would weaken its sovereignty.

The EU has taken a different course with Washington, reaching a trade agreement that set a 15% U.S. tariff ceiling on the vast majority of EU exports while Europe eliminated tariffs on U.S. industrial goods.

That contrast has loomed over Carney’s push for closer European ties. In a closely watched speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, he urged middle powers to work together to increase their leverage in an era of great-power rivalry.

“When we only negotiate bilaterally with a hegemon, we negotiate from weakness. We accept what is offered,” Carney said.

“This is not sovereignty,” he said. “It is the performance of sovereignty while accepting subordination.”

Carney’s Davos speech drew a personal rebuke from Trump, and von der Leyen's overture to America’s neighbor could raise the temperature again.

Barry Andrews, chair of the European Parliament’s Development Committee, called Canada “a perfect ally for Europe” and said closer ties could bring particular benefits for Ireland, noting that more than 10% of Canadians claim Irish ancestry.

__

Associated Press writer Sam McNeil in Brussels contributed to this report.

entries.title: Federal Reserve Raises Interest Rates for First Time in Three Years
entries.summary: The rate-setting committee cited elevated uncertainty due to “geopolitical developments” in its decision to finally raise rates after holding them steady since January.
entries.content:
The Federal Reserve raised interest rates on Wednesday for the first time since 2023 in an attempt to tamp down high inflation that’s heated up with the Iran war.

The Federal Open Market Committee voted 12-0 to hike rates to 3.75% to 4%, an increase of a quarter percentage point. Monetary policymakers cited solid economic and productivity growth, as well as job gains, in their announcement.

“While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient,” the statement read. “Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability.”

The vote was one of Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s greatest tests yet, as month-to-month inflation worsened and overwhelmed workers’ wage gains. President Donald Trump selected Warsh after publicly pressuring the previous Fed chair, Jerome Powell, to slash rates and insisting his new pick should do the same.

Trump doubled down on lowering rates as recently as Sunday.

“We should be paying the lowest interest rate in the world, regardless of their formulas,” Trump told reporters at the Irish Open golf tournament on Sunday.

The committee had punted the decision to change rates in every meeting since January, choosing instead to keep rates steady in part because the future of the Iran war remained unclear. But the Trump administration’s promises that the war would come to a quick end and energy prices would plummet have not come to bear. Economists’ expectations that the Fed would eventually raise rates soared.

Half of the members of the rate-setting committee — which includes the Fed’s seven board governors, the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and four rotating members from the Reserve Bank presidents — indicated in the committee’s June projections that they expected interest rates to rise this year. Warsh, a fierce critic of the Fed signaling its future moves to eager markets, sat out of that quarterly projection.

The Fed’s decision to raise interest rates will likely increase rates for mortgages, credit cards and auto loans. High rates also make borrowing money more expensive for businesses, increasing the likelihood of higher unemployment for the sake of limiting inflation.

Persistent inflation has long been a problem for the central bank, consistently topping the Fed’s 2% target inflation rate since the U.S. economy began climbing out of its pandemic slump.

The annual inflation rate in August came in at 3.4%, and month-to-month inflation increased 0.4% from July, according to a report released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics on Friday. Inflation has increased every month since May 2020, with the exception of a dip in June after the U.S. and Iran announced a short-lived ceasefire.

The Congressional Budget Office estimated that increased energy prices from the Iran war added a significant share to the inflation rate in the second quarter of 2026, according to a report released Tuesday. The CBO projects that energy prices will continue to add to inflation in the first months of 2027.

Investor anxiety over where the economy is headed has also manifested in the bond market. Yields — or the return on investment — for 10-year and 30-year U.S. Treasury notes hit their highest rates in decades in the last month. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has announced up to $6 billion in buyback purchases of government bonds, but the initiative has failed to rein in high yields.

entries.title: Commanders Unveil Interior Renderings of New Stadium
entries.summary: The plan includes a fan wall alongside one end zone and seeks to avoid any obstructed seats.
entries.content:
The Commanders are giving fans an inside look at their new stadium.

On Wednesday, in collaboration with design firm HKS, the team released renderings of the interior of the new stadium, which is set to open in 2030 on the site of the old RFK Stadium. The Commanders played at the site from 1961 to 1996 before moving to Northwest Stadium in Maryland in 1997.
https://x.com/Commanders/status/2100230760187703434The new stadium renderings appear to address some of the complaints about Northwest Stadium, especially concerning seats with obstructed views. The renderings show a unified seating bowl that’s designed “in one continuous sweep from field level to upper deck”, according to the release. The layout has no “stacked premium levels and minimal overhangs blocking sightlines or absorbing crowd noise.”

The renderings also include a fan wall alongside an end zone for the team’s diehard fans that will include affordable seating. Intuit Dome, the home of the NBA’s Los Angeles Clippers, opened in 2024 and has its own wall of fans which heckle opposing players and create visual distractions while they’re shooting free throws, similar to a college basketball arena.

The Commanders and HKS previously released exterior renderings that include a glass roof. The team is set to contribute $2.7 billion to the project, which also has $1.1 billion in taxpayer funding. The stadium is expected to seat roughly 65,000 fans. In July, the city sold the rights to the seats to the Commanders for no more than $975 million. The Commanders will sell personal seat licenses, according to the agreement to help pay for construction costs of the stadium.
Commanders interior renderings 2 (2560x1440, AR: 1.78)The stadium will be part of a mixed-use 180-acre area that will also include commercial space, housing units and parks. The complex is expected to generate $4 billion in tax revenue, but has drawn debate over how fans can efficiently commute in and out of the area once it’s built.

entries.title: Charlie Kirk's Family Blames Utah Officials for His Assassination
entries.summary: They filed a wrongful death notice, an action that presages a possible lawsuit.
entries.content:
By Hannah Schoenbaum and Matthew Brown

SALT LAKE CITY (AP) — Charlie Kirk’s family blamed Utah officials for failing to prevent the conservative activist’s assassination at a state university, in a wrongful death notice announced Wednesday that presages a possible lawsuit.

Attorneys for the family said Kirk's death resulted from a string of “reckless decisions” by officials at Utah Valley University that left him exposed to a rooftop sniper, who fired a fatal shot from more than 400 feet (122 meters) away on Sept. 10, 2025. The university has faced harsh criticism for a lack of key safety measures on the day of the shooting.

Kirk, 31, had been debating students in an outdoor courtyard surrounded by tall buildings and with several thousand people in attendance. An Associated Press review following the shooting showed the campus in Orem did not use several public safety practices that have become standard safeguards at events around the country.

Campus police staffing was far below recommended levels for a school of that size. They also did not fly a drone to monitor rooftops or coordinate with local law enforcement to secure the event attended by about 3,000 people. There were no bag checks or metal detectors.

“The risk of a rooftop shooter should have been especially top-of-mind given the attempted assassination of President Trump, Charlie Kirk’s close friend and political ally, by a rooftop shooter the previous year,” Kirk family attorney D. Loren Washburn wrote in the notice to state and university officials.

The document, dated Sept. 9, a day before the one-year anniversary of Kirk’s death, is a required step under state law before his family can file a formal claim or lawsuit. It names the university and its then-president, Astrid Tuminez; the campus police department and its chief, Jeffrey Long; and the state of Utah.

A spokesperson for Utah Valley University said the school was aware of the notice and would address it “consistent with our established processes.”

“Our focus remains on supporting our campus community,” spokesperson Sharon Turner said in a statement.

The Utah Attorney General’s Office said it does not comment on potential litigation.

Attorneys for Kirk's family alleged additional lapses by officials, including not conducting an adequate risk assessment before approving the event, failing to establish a secure perimeter and having no first responders immediately available, resulting in Kirk being taken to a nearby hospital in a private vehicle rather than an ambulance after he was shot.

“Tragically, the UVU Parties took none of these safety measures — steps only they had the authority to take — resulting in a situation that rendered Mr. Kirk helpless before his assassin,” Washburn wrote.

Long said after the shooting that six of his officers staffed the event and coordinated with Kirk’s eight-person private security team. The school said it was expanding its police force following the shooting.

Utah resident Tyler Robinson turned himself in a day after Kirk's killing. Prosecutors say he told his romantic partner that he “had enough of his (Kirk's) hatred.”

Robinson is charged with aggravated murder, making him eligible for the death penalty if convicted. A judge on Sept. 1 ordered the case to proceed toward trial. A date has not yet been set.

Prosecutors during a preliminary hearing in July presented what they characterized as overwhelming evidence against Robinson. That includes surveillance video of Robinson on the campus, DNA tests linking him to a rifle found near the assassination site and a handwritten note he allegedly left for his romantic partner that read, “I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk, and I took it.”

Kirk's parents, Robert and Kathryn Kirk, and widow, Erika Kirk, attended the hearings.

State law allows heirs or personal representatives of people who die to file lawsuits seeking damages if the death was caused by a wrongful act or negligence. The notice from Kirk’s family did not specify what damages they may seek.

entries.title: Inmates Sue Over Lack of Response to D.C. Jail Fire
entries.summary: A new lawsuit says it took hours for guards at a D.C. jail to respond to a 2023 incident.
entries.content:
It took hours for guards at a D.C. jail to respond to an incarcerated individual who repeatedly threatened to kill himself before ultimately starting an electrical fire in his cell, according to a lawsuit filed Monday.

The complaint, filed by five current and former inmates at the Central Detention Facility in Southeast D.C., said staff at the jail did not properly respond to the man’s cries or multiple fires he set during the 2023 incident. They are seeking an unspecified amount of money in damages.

The five inmates each suffered excessive smoke inhalation and significant psychological distress, according to the complaint filed in D.C. Superior Court.

After yelling for help overnight, the man lit pieces of paper and fabric on fire and pushed them out of his cell into the hallway. Flames burned on and off for nearly an hour while staff stood by, the complaint said.

“I thought that the officers were going to let us burn alive,” Noah Summers, one of the five men suing, said in a statement. “We all banged on our doors, and nobody came for hours.”

They claim staff didn’t intervene as the man dragged an electric box fan into his cell, starting an electric fire which blanketed the area with thick, black smoke. Shortly after the fire started, a guard used a fire extinguisher to douse the flames and inmates in the unit were evacuated through a smoky hallway, the complaint said.

The men were all housed in the facility’s mental health unit at the time of the fire. Two are still at the Central Detention Facility, two are in the federal prison system and one lives at a residential treatment program in the District.

Part of the complaint has been redacted to protect internal jail records.

The lawsuit also claims the D.C. Department of Corrections failed to properly train and supervise staff, leading to mishandling of the incident. A report from the D.C. Auditor’s Office released in May 2025 found “inadequate staff training,” among other issues, impacted the well-being and safety of inmates in D.C. jails.

entries.title: Burgum Reveals Plans to Install 12 Signs Outside the Smithsonian’s American History Museum
entries.summary: The Trump administration has accused the institution of anti-American bias.
entries.content:
The Interior Department is planning to install roughly a dozen signs outside the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History that will denounce certain exhibits, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said in a letter to two senators.

Each sign will cost about $7,000 and their contents are still being finalized, Burgum wrote to Sens. Jeff Merkley (D-Oregon) and Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) earlier this month. The correspondence came in response to an Aug. 6 inquiry about the implementation of President Donald Trump’s executive order directing the Cabinet official to install temporary displays outside the building.

The previously undisclosed letter was first reported Tuesday evening by The Atlantic.

The executive order is part of Trump’s larger efforts to reshape the Smithsonian Institution as he pushes back against what he calls “a revisionist movement.” He has accused the National Museum of American History of prioritizing “woke” and unpatriotic displays and sought to exert greater control over the Smithsonian by levying financial pressure, despite the fact that he has no direct oversight of the independent agency.

“The purpose of these signs is straightforward: Americans should enter the NMAH with relevant information about the curators’ interpretation of history and their stated goal of changing the viewpoints of visitors to the museum,” Burgum said in his letter.

Merkley called the signs “another step” in the Trump administration’s plans to undermine the Smithsonian’s integrity. Murkowski and Merkley are the leaders of the Senate Interior-Environment Appropriations Subcommittee, which has jurisdiction over the Smithsonian’s funding.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“I’ll fight like hell to protect the Smithsonian’s independence so that the Institution can continue to tell all of America’s story for generations to come,” Merkley said in a statement Wednesday.

In his letter, Burgum listed several examples of programming he found to “advance ideologies that distract from a coherent and accurate presentation of America’s story,” including displays that reference undocumented immigrants and transgender people.

Burgum argued that such material could offend military families and federal law enforcement by legitimizing “illegal immigration and open borders.” Parents of young children, Burgum added, should also be “equipped to protect the well-being of their children” by knowing that some exhibits present “ideological viewpoints inconsistent with biology.”

“We believe the public should enter the museum fully equipped with the information needed to evaluate whether to invest their time viewing these exhibits and programming,” Burgum wrote. “These signs will do just that.”

Lonnie Bunch, secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, has steadily defended the agency’s independence amid criticism from the Trump administration. The institution’s top leader, who has spent his career promoting a more nuanced version of American history that features both its successes and failures, announced earlier in September that he would step down at the end of the year. Bunch told The New York Times the move was not in response to White House pressure.

Murkowski told The Washington Sun on Wednesday that she was a “big fan” of Bunch’s leadership at the Smithsonian, which she said has already undergone a “very critical review of the displays and the descriptions” following a mandate from Trump.

“I think it's unfortunate that you have some in the administration who now feel that they would put additional signs on the exterior,” Murkowski said. “I've asked, ‘Where do you get the money out of your budget to do all of this?’ I haven't gotten a straight answer back on that.”

Igor Bobic contributed to this report.

entries.title: Global Poll Finds Declining Comfort With the U.S. as a World Leader
entries.summary: The poll comes as the U.S. remains engaged in several conflicts across the world.
entries.content:
A new global poll found declining comfort with either the United States and China taking a leading role in world affairs, even as support for international cooperation remained steady.

Just 39% of respondents said they were comfortable with the United States playing a leading role in global affairs, and 37% were comfortable with China, according to a Rockefeller Foundation survey. The poll surveyed 35,399 adults across 34 countries from July 21 to Aug. 5.

Canada received the highest level of support, at 60%, followed by Japan at 58% and Australia at 55%. Also, 61% of respondents said they would support countries working together to address global problems even if the group did not include the U.S. or China.

Respondents expressed broader pessimism about the state of the world. Nearly 7 in 10 said the world had gotten worse over the past year, while 57% said countries should cooperate to address global challenges even when doing so requires compromising some national interests.

The poll comes as the United States remains engaged in a war with Iran and trade disputes with Canada, while the Israel-Hamas conflict continues to shape debate over U.S. foreign policy and the Middle East. 

The survey also found growing trust in several international institutions. Some 69% of people said they trust in the World Health Organization, up from 61% last year, while trust in the United Nations increased 4 percentage points to 62%, according to the foundation.

The findings come as the U.S. government has pulled back from several international institutions it historically helped lead.

In January 2025, the Trump administration announced it would be pulling out of the WHO due to disagreements over the institution’s handling of COVID-19, China’s alleged influence over the body and the United States’ financial obligations.

The administration has used the same reasoning to attack the U.N.

"The United Nations is funding an assault on Western countries and their borders. ... The U.N. is supposed to stop invasions, not create them and not finance them," President Donald Trump said in his 2025 speech before the body.
entries.author: Raymond Fernández

entries.title: Bill Cassidy Says He’s Fed Up With Trump Nominees’ ‘Wiggle Room’ on Vaccines
entries.summary: The Louisiana Republican repeatedly pressed Trump’s surgeon general nominee on whether she believes vaccines cause autism.
entries.content:
Sen. Bill Cassidy lambasted the Trump administration for stoking vaccine doubts among Americans, after reports Tuesday that two unvaccinated Pennsylvanians had died of measles.

“It is irresponsible, it damages our country, and we have four people in Pennsylvania reportedly dead because of that sort of activity,” the Louisiana Republican said at a Wednesday Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee hearing to confirm President Donald Trump’s surgeon general pick, Nicole Saphier.

It was Cassidy’s latest opportunity to air his grievances against Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for undermining confidence in childhood vaccines as measles cases grow to their highest levels in decades.

The deaths — and initially conflicting reports over whether all were caused by measles — have fueled public sparring between Kennedy and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, further fueled by recent news that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention isn’t adding the deaths to its measles database.

“It is … deeply concerning to learn that the Secretary personally intervened in an otherwise administrative process to direct the CDC to not report these Pennsylvania deaths, presumably because it doesn’t fit his phony narrative,” Shapiro, a Democrat, wrote Tuesday on X.

Cassidy expressed frustration Wednesday at Saphier’s responses when he drilled her on whether vaccines cause autism, an idea contradicted by decades of research but which Trump aired at an Oval Office event last month.

“I don’t know what causes autism … but I have not seen evidence that vaccines cause autism,” Saphier responded.

“There is a little bit of wiggle room there,” Cassidy cut in. “I am so sensitive to this.”

The lone Republican willing to sharply criticize the administration’s approach to vaccination, Cassidy, who chairs the HELP committee, will leave Congress at the end of the year after losing his primary to a Trump-backed candidate.

Trump’s health nominees have had to answer for the administration’s efforts to roll back childhood vaccine recommendations and for claims by Trump and Kennedy that some vaccines should be viewed with suspicion.

Trump called the combination measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine — given to millions of children every year — “quite lethal” last month as he signed an executive order instructing the Department of Health and Human Services to reduce the childhood vaccine schedule.

“I can tell you that I do not believe the MMR vaccine to be lethal,” Saphier told Cassidy.

“I appreciate the president is trying to reach the vaccine-hesitant people who are wanting more answers or who are concerned that there are too many doses,” she added.

Cassidy shot back: “I’m not sure the way to reach people with vaccine hesitancy is by feeding into untruths.”

The senator has expressed support for Saphier, who is Trump’s second surgeon general pick after his first one failed to gain enough GOP support, but he hasn’t said whether he’ll vote to confirm her.

Wednesday’s hearing didn’t include Heidi Overton, Trump’s nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration. Overton, who advises the White House on domestic policy, stood next to Trump in the Oval Office as he signed the executive order on the vaccine schedule.

A committee spokesman said the panel received Overton’s paperwork Tuesday and is working with the administration to schedule her confirmation hearing.

entries.title: Josh Shapiro and RFK Jr. Return to Sniping at Each Other After Two More Measles Deaths
entries.summary: The two new deaths bring Pennsylvania’s measles-associated death toll to four as Shapiro and Kennedy clash over the federal response to the outbreak.
entries.content:
Pennsylvania’s announcement of two additional measles-associated deaths has renewed a public dispute between Gov. Josh Shapiro and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who have been sparring over public health measures in the state for weeks.

The deaths bring the state’s total to four this year — its first measles-associated deaths in 35 years. Pennsylvania has recorded 693 cases across 38 counties, the state’s Department of Health confirmed.

“This serious situation continues to be made worse by RFK Jr. playing games with public health and safety,” Gov. Shapiro said in a social media post Tuesday. “It's long past time for [Secretary Kennedy] to stop stoking vaccine skepticism and misinformation and compromising the serious mission of the nation’s public health agencies.”

The latest clash centers in part on how the deaths are being counted at the federal level. Shapiro accused Kennedy of intervening in the CDC’s reporting process after earlier Pennsylvania deaths were not initially reflected in the agency’s national tally.

Kennedy has denied directing the CDC to withhold the deaths from its statistics, saying the agency is following its standard for determining when measles is listed as the underlying cause of death.

“Governor Shapiro has chosen to politicize this outbreak instead of implementing a unified public health response,” Kennedy responded on X. “He continues to point the finger at me and the federal government.”

Kennedy criticized Pennsylvania for not requesting a CDC Epi-Aid, which would send federal epidemiologists into the state to investigate the outbreak. He also said Pennsylvania had declined federal assistance.

Lancaster County, home to one of the largest Amish communities in the country, has been hardest hit by the outbreak. Nearly half of the state’s measles cases have been reported there, making it particularly risky since vaccination rates among the Amish are incredibly low.

Kennedy has accused Shapiro of shifting blame to the Amish community.

Shapiro and Kennedy’s feud began after the governor denounced the secretary’s vaccination messaging when he announced the first two measles-related deaths in the state in over 35 years.

In a call before Shapiro’s announcement, Kennedy offered federal assistance to control the outbreak, but they each had different accounts of the conversation. Kennedy said Shapiro acknowledged the vaccination rates had declined under the Biden administration, which the governor denied. And Shapiro said he told the secretary his negative rhetoric on vaccines was harming people in the state and implored him to encourage vaccinations.
entries.author: Raymond Fernández

entries.title: Kennedy Center's CFO Resigned on Day Board Voted to Close: Report
entries.summary: Donna Kauranen resigned on the same day the Kennedy Center board voted to close the institution for proposed renovations.
entries.content:
The Kennedy Center’s chief financial officer, Donna Kauranen, resigned from her position on Tuesday, according to reports. The resignation came the same day the board of trustees voted to close the center down for renovations and add President Donald Trump’s name to the building.

Kauranen’s resignation was first reported by NBC News, which cited two people familiar with the matter. The Kennedy Center did not respond to a request for comment from The Washington Sun.

It remains unclear whether the renovations will move forward. Trump said after Tuesday’s board meeting that he would not approve the proposed construction unless his name is added to the building.

The board, which Trump stocked with allies in 2025 after taking over as chairman, also voted Tuesday on proposed designs for re-adding his name to the Kennedy Center.

The developments came as a legal battle continues between Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center board, and the institution’s leadership. Hours before Tuesday’s meeting, U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper ruled that the board could not circumvent his earlier decision blocking the addition of Trump’s name and an initial plan to close the center for renovations.

Kauranen was appointed Kennedy Center CFO in March 2025, around the time the Trump administration began reshaping the institution’s leadership. Before joining the Kennedy Center, she held budget and financial positions on a handful of gubernatorial campaigns.

entries.title: House Republicans Cut Their Work Week Short and Avoid Hegseth Impeachment Vote
entries.summary: After members depart D.C. on Wednesday, they are not scheduled to reconvene until after the November midterm elections.
entries.content:
House Republicans have opted to cut their workweek short by one day, holding their last votes Wednesday rather than Thursday and avoiding a contentious, longshot vote on whether to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

House Republican leadership had already canceled the last two weeks of September votes. After members depart Wednesday, they will not return until after the November midterm elections.

Speaker Mike Johnson denied that the change in schedule was due to the privileged motion made by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky) on Tuesday to impeach Hegseth. Johnson would have had to put Hegseth’s impeachment up for consideration by Thursday, because privileged motions must be taken up within two days of being introduced.

“It's a publicity stunt by someone who wants attention,” Johnson said of Massie’s impeachment motion. “It will immediately be tabled, of course, but we probably won't do that today. We'll probably do it when we come back.”

A contempt motion recommended by the House Oversight Committee against billionaire investor Leon Black for defying subpoenas related to the Jeffrey Epstein investigation “probably moves today, and I think it'll move pretty quickly,” Johnson said Wednesday.

He said House lawmakers have already done their job, “so it's time for our members to go home to their districts and make their case to the American people to go and explain all the great things we've done.”

The speaker added that the House passed more than 70 bills this week alone and has passed hundreds of pieces of legislation this session — though many of those bills are now waiting to be picked up in the Senate.

“The House has done so much of that for the last 19, 20 months or so, and a lot of it is just awaiting action in the Senate,” Johnson said — adding that he would bring the House back on 48 hours’ notice “if the Senate works together and moves some of these important pieces of legislation.”

With less than 50 days until the Nov. 3 elections, House lawmakers are now set to return home to their districts.

entries.title: DMV High School Volleyball Players of Week 2
entries.summary: This week’s group features standouts from Madison, Richard Montgomery and St. John’s.
entries.content:
With another week of volleyball matches in the books, the DMV’s top teams and talent are starting to emerge. Here are three players who stepped up in early September:

Katie Mitchell, Junior, Outside Hitter, Richard Montgomery

Mitchell is one of the buzziest prospects in the area this fall. The 6-foot-1 outside hitter is committed to Minnesota and ranked as a Top 100 recruit by PrepDig. Mitchell has lived up to that billing for the Rockets, who are off to an undefeated start. Mitchell racked up double-digit kills in each of her team’s first three matches, including a 22-kill outburst against 4A state finalist Urbana and a 17-kill performance against rival Churchill, which took down the Rockets in last year’s state quarterfinals.

“Katie’s a super strong player, knowledgeable about the game — she’s definitely a presence to play against and also to play with,” coach Gretchen Barber-Strunk said. “I think our girls have an advantage in getting to practice with her. … If you can dig a ball from Katie, that’s pretty much the hardest you’re going to see.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Laila Chadwick, Senior, Outside Hitter, Madison

Chadwick is committed to Oklahoma to play libero, but she’s spending her final season at Madison crushing kills as an outside hitter. Standing at just 5-foot-8, the senior uses an impressive vertical leap to lead her team’s offense from the outside. The Warhawks, who dealt with an injury bug in the opening month of their season, have relied heavily on Chadwick’s offense. She racked up 76 kills and 10 service aces in Madison’s first five matches of the season. In early September, Chadwick led the Warhawks to a thrilling 3-2 victory over Flint Hill, a longtime power in the Independent School League. With Chadwick in charge, the Warhawks are poised to make a deep run with the hopes of winning their first state title since 2015.

“She’s insanely athletic … you would never guess stat-wise that she’s not super tall,” Madison coach Kendal Hall said. “We’re excited to have her for one last year.”

Gabrielle Deutz, Senior, Setter, St. John’s

St. John’s coach Bill Pribac likened the setter position to the quarterback of a football team. Deutz has played that role masterfully for the Cadets, who have already picked up five wins and look to be a viable contender in the Washington Catholic Athletic Conference. In her team’s season opener against National Cathedral, Deutz tallied 32 assists in a commanding three-set victory. She’s also made her mark serving the ball, notching a team-high five aces in that same match. She topped that performance with seven aces against St. John’s Catholic Prep two matches later.

“Her serve has been uncanny this year,” Pribac said. “She’s definitely been very consistent.”

entries.title: Capitals Hand Out Two 8-Year Contracts Just Before CBA Deadline
entries.summary: Washington signed Ryan Leonard and Justin Sourdif hours before a new collective bargaining agreement took effect.
entries.content:
The Capitals locked in two young pieces of their offense for the long haul Tuesday, just hours before a critical deadline.

The team re-signed forward Ryan Leonard and right winger Justin Sourdif to 8-year contracts on the final day such deals were eligible under the NHL’s collective bargaining agreement. The CBA changed at midnight Wednesday and now allows players to extend for up to seven years, meaning both of Washington’s deals may be the last of their kind.

Leonard’s deal is worth $84 million with an average annual value of $10.5 million. Sourdif’s is worth $50.8 million with an average annual value of $6.35 million. Both contracts will start next summer and were part of a long list of similar Tuesday deals from across the league as teams looked to lock in young talent ahead of a new season. The Capitals open training camp on Thursday.

Leonard, 21, was the No. 8 pick in the 2023 NHL draft and finished last season with 20 goals and 45 points, becoming the first Capitals rookie to score 20 goals since Alex Ovechkin in 2005–06. The Capitals decided to give Leonard a long-term deal after playing just 84 games for the team.

“Ryan is a young and talented player who is still years away from entering his prime, and we believe he has tremendous potential to continue growing into an important player for our organization,” Senior Vice President and General Manager Chris Patrick said in a release. “While reaching his full potential will take time, we have been impressed with his work ethic and the way he continues to develop his game.”

Sourdif was also a rookie last season at 24. The Capitals acquired him from the Florida Panthers a day before the 2025 draft. Patrick pivoted to extending Sourdif after finishing Leonard’s deal.

“Once we got things squared away with Ryan, I just gave Justin’s agent a call and talked about how he wanted to move forward going into the season, and [asked] is this something he wants to continue having discussions on, or does he want to just let the season play out?” Patrick said in a separate release announcing Sourdif’s deal.

“And as the day went on, it became apparent that they were definitely willing to explore an eight-year deal if we could find something that made sense for them. And they definitely were very open to working with us to make a deal. I was really appreciative of that, and really happy that he was willing to stick with it and work with us here in the 11th hour.”

A native of British Columbia, Sourdif started last season on the Capitals’ fourth line and saw his playing time gradually increase over the course of the season. He finished the year with 15 goals and 20 assists and, like Leonard, was set to be a restricted free agent at the end of this coming season.
